<section class="proj-q" aria-labelledby="h-question">
<h2 id="h-question"><i class="bi bi-question-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Research question</h2>
<p class="proj-question">Can multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression, combining a theoretical power curve with limited measured data, improve probabilistic wind turbine power-curve estimation?</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-insight" id="insight" aria-labelledby="h-insight">
<h2 id="h-insight"><i class="bi bi-stars" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key insight</h2>
<p class="insight-title">A theoretical power curve helped, but the gain depended on the metric</p>
<p>The method fuses about two hundred sampled measurements with the theoretical power curve of the turbine type, which covers all wind speeds but does not show how a turbine actually runs. In the reported nine-turbine test, nonlinear multi-fidelity regression had a lower RMSE than standard Gaussian process regression for most turbines, but the ranking depended on the evaluation metric.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-explainer" id="explainer" aria-labelledby="h-explainer">
<h2 id="h-explainer"><i class="bi bi-sliders" aria-hidden="true"></i>How does a theoretical curve help a few measurements?</h2>
<div class="explainer" data-explainer="uq-mfgpr">
<p class="ex-fallback">A Gaussian process fitted to a few measured points is uncertain wherever the points are sparse, so its band widens between them. A multi-fidelity model also learns from the turbine&#x27;s theoretical power curve, which covers every wind speed, and uses it to fill in the shape between measurements, so the band can narrow there. In the paper&#x27;s test, the result depended on the evaluation metric.</p>
</div>
<p class="ex-note"><i class="bi bi-info-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study&#x27;s data or results.</p>
</section>

<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-contribution">
<h2 id="h-contribution"><i class="bi bi-person-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>My contribution</h2>
<p>First author. Implemented and evaluated the models, with funding from the U.S. Department of Energy through the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="approach" aria-labelledby="h-approach">
<h2 id="h-approach"><i class="bi bi-tools" aria-hidden="true"></i>How I approached it</h2>
<ol class="approach">
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Measured SCADA records show real behaviour, including scatter, stops and curtailment, but are noisy and very numerous.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I drew a few hundred representative points from a kernel density estimate of the records, which keeps the shape of the scatter without manual cleaning.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>A Gaussian process solve grows with the cube of the training points, so a compact training set matters.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>The theoretical curve covers every wind speed but not how a turbine actually operates.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I compared linear and nonlinear multi-fidelity models, which link the curve to the measurements, with a standard Gaussian process on measurements alone, on point and probabilistic metrics.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>Testing both kinds of metric showed that the gain depended on which error matters.</p></li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-method">
<h2 id="h-method"><i class="bi bi-diagram-3" aria-hidden="true"></i>Method</h2>
<p>Linear (autoregressive) and nonlinear multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression that fuse the turbine type&#x27;s theoretical power curve (low fidelity) with a few hundred kernel-density-sampled SCADA points from the open SDWPF dataset (high fidelity), compared with single-fidelity regression on point and probabilistic metrics.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-findings">
<h2 id="h-findings"><i class="bi bi-lightbulb" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key findings</h2>
<ol class="findings">
<li>In the reported nine-turbine test, nonlinear multi-fidelity regression achieved lower RMSE for most turbines; performance depended on the evaluation metric.</li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-bounds" aria-labelledby="h-bounds">
<h2 id="h-bounds"><i class="bi bi-exclamation-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Boundary conditions</h2>
<p>One dataset and one generic low-fidelity curve.</p>
</section>
